power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We conducted a series of power analyses to determine an appropriate number of both countries (K = 20, 25, 30, 32) and participants per country (N = 150, 200, 250, 300). To assess the expected power, we set α = .05. We used the simr package in R to run 1,000 simulations of the planned mixed-models specified in our analysis plan 47 . Model parameters were estimated based on previous literature and our pilot study. The simulations utilized the Kenward-Roger approximation for fixed effects testing to ensure robustness. See the Supplementary Information for power curves for both hypotheses across the full parameter space.
table.statistical_test_other: mixed models with Kenward-Roger approximation for fixed effects

table.text: Table 1. Design table Hypotheses Outcome Measures Sampling Plan (N, power analyses) Analysis Plan Interpretation H1 (country-level): individuals from countries higher in emotional expressivity will show stronger emotion overgeneralization, such that the association between happinessresemblance scores and trustworthiness ratings will be stronger. DV: Individual Fisher z-transformed emotion overgeneralization (participant-level Pearson r between happinessresemblance scores of 120 face stimuli and trustworthiness ratings, Fisher ztransformed). Predictor: countrylevel mean emotional expressivity (Abridged Display Rule Assessment Inventory). 32 countries (K = 32), 200 participants/country (N ≈ 6,400). Power analysis via simr (1,000 simulations, α = .05) shows 95.2% power to detect b = 0.16 for the Level-2 predictor. Power for Level-2 effects is primarily driven by K rather than N; K = 32 is substantial by cross-cultural standards. Stratified by gender, age (18-65), region within country; recruited via online panel providers. Multilevel linear model, individuals (L1) nested in countries (L2). DV: Fisher z overgeneralization. Predictor: country-mean expressivity (L2). Covariates: age, gender (L1); ethnic fractionalization (L2). Random intercepts for country. Robustness checks: recompute overgeneralization within each face-race subset (White/Black/Latino/As ian); re-run using CFD norming data as alternative happinessresemblance proxy. Positive: supports the prediction that countrylevel expressivity is associated with stronger overgeneralization, consistent with ecological calibration. Null: no evidence for a cross-cultural expressivityovergeneralization link; interpreted as lack of support for countrylevel calibration. Negative: contradicts the proposed direction, suggesting different ecological dynamics than hypothesized. H2 (individuallevel): Within countries, individuals with greater emotional expressivity will show stronger emotion overgeneralization. Same DV as H1. Predictors: groupmean centered individual expressivity (withincountry effect) and country-mean expressivity (between-country control). Same dataset as H1. Power via simr (1,000 simulations, α = .05) exceeds 95% to detect a small effect (b = 0.10) at K = 32, N = 200, under a conservative random-slope-variance assumption (0.0144, allowing ~20% of countries to show a reversed association). Multilevel model. DV: Fisher z overgeneralization. Predictor: group-mean centered individual expressivity (withincountry); country-mean expressivity (betweencountry covariate). Covariates: age, gender (L1); ethnic fractionalization (L2). Random effects for country (maximal structure attempted; simplified to random intercepts only if convergence fails). Robustness checks: same as H1. Positive within-country effect: supports the individual-level internalization account-individual differences in perceived expressivity predict overgeneralization even net of country. Null: no evidence that perceived norms relate to overgeneralization within countries; consistent with a more invariant account at the individual level. Negative: contradicts the proposed direction, suggesting alternative mechanisms or measurement issues.

We conducted simulation-based power analyses using the simr package in R 47, following the planned multilevel models described in the main text. Analyses were implemented using R scripts adapted from prior work 53, with modifications to match the present design. Full simulation code and output tables are provided to facilitate reproducibility (see the Code Availability section).

We conducted a sensitivity analysis by varying the effect size (b = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15) and the random slope variance for expressivity (0.0064, 0.0144, 0.0256). We specifically tested a slope variance of 0.0144 (SD = 0.12) as a conservative estimate; this value accounts for potential cultural heterogeneity where approximately 20% of countries might theoretically exhibit an association in the opposite direction. At K = 32 and N = 200, we achieved power > 95% for a small effect of b = 0.10 even under a conservative variance assumption of 0.0144 (Figure S4).

table.header: Assessment of cross-cultural variability in perceptual mapping

table.text: All simulations used 1,000 iterations, with statistical significance evaluated at α = .05 and fixed effects tested using the Kenward-Roger approximation. Power was estimated across a range of design parameters, including the number of countries (K = 20, 25, 30, 32), the number of participants per country (N = 150, 200, 250, 300), and plausible effect sizes informed by pilot data and prior literature. For H1, the primary simulation used an expected effect of b = 0.16, based on the pilot study. For H2, we additionally varied the random slope variance for individual-level expressivity (0.0064, 0.0144, 0.0256), corresponding to slope standard deviations of 0.08, 0.12, and 0.16.

All simulations used 1,000 iterations, with statistical significance evaluated at α = .05 and fixed effects tested using the Kenward-Roger approximation. Power was estimated across a range of design parameters, including the number of countries (K = 20, 25, 30, 32), the number of participants per country (N = 150, 200, 250, 300), and plausible effect sizes informed by pilot data and prior literature. For H1, the primary simulation used an expected effect of b = 0.16, based on the pilot study. For H2, we additionally varied the random slope variance for individual-level expressivity (0.0064, 0.0144, 0.0256), corresponding to slope standard deviations of 0.08, 0.12, and 0.16.

Power curves for H2 across parameter space. Estimated statistical power for detecting the effect of individual-level expressivity on overgeneralization as a function of random slope variance and number of countries (K). Panels are arranged by effect size (b; rows) and number of participants per country (N; columns). Points represent mean power across 1,000 simulations, with vertical lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Horizontal dashed and dotted lines denote 95% and 90% power thresholds, respectively. Under the planned design (K = 32, N = 200), power exceeded 95% for detecting a small effect (b = 0.10) under a conservative slope variance assumption (0.0144). Curves for K = 30 are omitted for visual clarity; this condition was included in the simulations but is not shown in the figure.

In sum, these simulations suggest that a sample of 200 participants per country across 32 countries (N = 6,400) provides sufficient power to detect our primary effects of interest. This target ensures we are well-powered for individual-level effects while maintaining a rigorous and feasible sample for country-level comparisons.

For H1, we examined the effect of country-level expressivity on face-based overgeneralization. As this hypothesis involves a level-2 predictor, power is primarily driven by the number of countries (K) rather than the number of participants (N). With K = 30 and N = 200, the estimated power was 93.6%, slightly below the prespecified 95% threshold. We therefore increased the number of countries to K = 32, which yielded 95.2% power for this effect (Figure S3). K = 32 is also comparable to, or larger than, those commonly used in cross-cultural psychological research 48, 49.

Panels are arranged by effect size (b; rows) and number of participants per country (N; columns). Points represent mean power across 1,000 simulations, with vertical lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Horizontal dashed and dotted lines denote 95% and 90% power thresholds, respectively. Under the planned design (K = 32, N = 200), power exceeded 95% for detecting a small effect (b = 0.10) under a conservative slope variance assumption (0.0144). Curves for K = 30 are omitted for visual clarity; this condition was included in the simulations but is not shown in the figure.", "In sum, these simulations suggest that a sample of 200 participants per country across 32 countries (N = 6,400) provides sufficient power to detect our primary effects of interest. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 50 columns across 6 data files.
#### Issues Identified

1 file/column combination has at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = "facerating_raw.csv", Column = "user_id", Issues = "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: userid)"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 6 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 5 R code files.
#### Run order

No ordering signal (no data dependency, `source()` call, or numeric filename prefix) distinguishes the run order of these files. They may need to run in a specific order that could not be determined automatically — check this before running.

), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—", "—", "—"), Basis = c("none", 
"none", "none", "none", "none")), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = "data.frame")

```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 5 scripts: 2 ran without error, 0 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **2 scripts need a person** to choose a file, answer a question or use an app, which cannot be reproduced without one: pilot_analysis.R, pilot_analysis.Rmd. Naming the file in the script solves this.

text.text: Judgments of trustworthiness from faces guide critical social decisions.
It remains debated whether these judgments reflect shared features of human perception or are shaped by cultural experience.
One prominent explanation is emotion overgeneralization: faces that structurally resemble emotional expressions elicit corresponding impressions, even when no emotion is displayed.
Although often treated as universal, emotion overgeneralization may reflect ecological learning shaped by culture-specific norms.
We propose a cultural gradient: where emotional expressions are more informative, the link between happiness resemblance and perceived trustworthiness should be stronger.

Participants from 32 countries (N ≈ 6,400) will evaluate the trustworthiness of unfamiliar individuals from standardized resting facial photographs and complete a measure of emotional expressivity, with each face's resemblance to happiness quantified computationally.
We will test whether emotional expressivity is associated with greater emotion overgeneralization at both country and individual levels.
Null results would favor perceptual invariance, whereas positive associations would support ecological calibration.
Judgments of trustworthiness are fundamental to human life, serving as a cornerstone for social cooperation and collective action 1, 2 .
text.formatted: Judgments of trustworthiness are fundamental to human life, serving as a cornerstone for social cooperation and collective action <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: Facial appearances shape these judgments, with perceivers forming stable impressions after only brief exposure 3 .
text.formatted: Facial appearances shape these judgments, with perceivers forming stable impressions after only brief exposure <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: These facial impressions can override more valid behavior information 4 , and predict various high-stakes outcomes, ranging from consumer decisions to criminal sentencing [5] [6] [7] .
text.formatted: These facial impressions can override more valid behavior information <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> , and predict various high-stakes outcomes, ranging from consumer decisions to criminal sentencing <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> .

text.text: Although trustworthiness judgments from faces have been studied extensively, they are typically treated as reflecting universal perceptual processes, with limited consideration of whether their magnitude is shaped by social ecology.

This issue reflects a long-standing question in social perception: to what extent are person perception processes shared across humans, and to what extent are they shaped by the cultural and ecological environments in which people develop?
Evidence for both perspectives has accumulated.

On one hand, analyses of a large-scale dataset found little systematic variation in facial trait impressions across world regions, suggesting that individual differences, rather than cultural background, account for the meaningful variation in impressions 8 .
text.formatted: On one hand, analyses of a large-scale dataset found little systematic variation in facial trait impressions across world regions, suggesting that individual differences, rather than cultural background, account for the meaningful variation in impressions <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> .

text.text: Similarly, the basic structure of social judgments appears to be relatively consistent across regions 9 .
text.formatted: Similarly, the basic structure of social judgments appears to be relatively consistent across regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: On the other hand, other work has identified variation in social perception associated with cultural and environmental factors.

For example, the structure of face impressions varies with regional personality profiles 10 , while individual differences in face-based trust evaluations are shaped more strongly by environmental than genetic factors 11.
text.formatted: For example, the structure of face impressions varies with regional personality profiles <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> , while individual differences in face-based trust evaluations are shaped more strongly by environmental than genetic factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref>.

text.text: Thus, cross-cultural similarity in social impressions does not necessarily imply that the processes underlying these impressions operate with equal strength.
Addressing these mixed findings requires theory-driven predictions about when and why social-perceptual processes should vary across cultures.

One prominent mechanism underlying face-based trustworthiness impressions is emotion overgeneralization, a bias grounded in the classic overgeneralization account whereby perceivers interpret momentary characteristics of a person as enduring traits 12 .
text.formatted: One prominent mechanism underlying face-based trustworthiness impressions is emotion overgeneralization, a bias grounded in the classic overgeneralization account whereby perceivers interpret momentary characteristics of a person as enduring traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Driven by an oversensitive emotion detection system, this bias extends beyond overt expressions to subtle structural facial resemblances [13] [14] [15] .
text.formatted: Driven by an oversensitive emotion detection system, this bias extends beyond overt expressions to subtle structural facial resemblances <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> .

text.text: For example, an individual with an emotionally "neutral" (resting) face resembling happy expressions is judged as more trustworthy 16, 17 , and computational approaches identified emotional resemblance as the strongest predictor of trustworthiness judgments 18.
text.formatted: For example, an individual with an emotionally "neutral" (resting) face resembling happy expressions is judged as more trustworthy <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> , and computational approaches identified emotional resemblance as the strongest predictor of trustworthiness judgments <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref>.

text.text: Emotion overgeneralization has been observed across diverse populations, showing that people across cultures spontaneously derive trait impressions from emotional cues 19 .
text.formatted: Emotion overgeneralization has been observed across diverse populations, showing that people across cultures spontaneously derive trait impressions from emotional cues <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> .

text.text: Influential accounts have treated emotion overgeneralization as a species-typical perceptual tendency shared across humans, emphasizing its universality [20] [21] [22].
text.formatted: Influential accounts have treated emotion overgeneralization as a species-typical perceptual tendency shared across humans, emphasizing its universality <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: However, cross-cultural presence does not imply invariance in magnitude.
Existing evidence is drawn predominantly from U.S. samples, where emotional expressions tend to be frequent and socially informative.
We extend this perspective: we propose that, although the underlying perceptual tendency may be universal, its strength is shaped by ecological experience.
Emotion overgeneralization may reflect ecological learning: social-perceptual systems are calibrated to cues that reliably predict important social outcomes within a given environment 23, 24.
text.formatted: Emotion overgeneralization may reflect ecological learning: social-perceptual systems are calibrated to cues that reliably predict important social outcomes within a given environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref>.

text.text: Emotional expressions provide such cues because they often signal others' intentions.

Positive affective states are associated with prosocial tendencies 25, 26 , and smiles, for example, can signal approachability and cooperative intent, whereas negative expressions can signal potential threat 21, 22, 24 .
text.formatted: Positive affective states are associated with prosocial tendencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> , and smiles, for example, can signal approachability and cooperative intent, whereas negative expressions can signal potential threat <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> .

text.text: Through repeated experience, individuals learn associations between emotional expressions and underlying intentions, and these learned associations can generalize to resting faces that share similar structural features 13 .
text.formatted: Through repeated experience, individuals learn associations between emotional expressions and underlying intentions, and these learned associations can generalize to resting faces that share similar structural features <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: The strength of these associations, however, should depend on the frequency and reliability of expression-intention pairings in a given ecology.
Supporting this, real-world face-based trait inference is malleable to the statistical learning of cooccurrence of facial appearances and behavioral outcomes 27.
text.formatted: Supporting this, real-world face-based trait inference is malleable to the statistical learning of cooccurrence of facial appearances and behavioral outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref>.

text.text: Emotional expressivity represents one important ecological factor shaping these learning environments.
Defined as the extent to which emotional states are normatively encouraged to be openly displayed 28 , expressivity influences both the frequency and interpretability of emotional signals.
text.formatted: Defined as the extent to which emotional states are normatively encouraged to be openly displayed <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> , expressivity influences both the frequency and interpretability of emotional signals.

text.text: In cultures where emotional expressions are normatively encouraged and reliably reflect authentic internal states, individuals encounter more frequent and consistent pairings between expressions and underlying intentions, strengthening the learned association between emotional cues and social judgments.
In contrast, when emotional displays are more regulated or contextdependent, expressions may provide less reliable information about internal states, weakening their diagnostic value.
Supporting this possibility, cultures differ in the social meanings of smiles.
Smiles can reflect pleasure, affiliation, or dominance, and the relative prominence of these functions varies across cultures 29, 30 .
text.formatted: Smiles can reflect pleasure, affiliation, or dominance, and the relative prominence of these functions varies across cultures <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> .

text.text: Smiling at strangers leads to good impressions in some countries, but impressions of lower competence in others 31 .
text.formatted: Smiling at strangers leads to good impressions in some countries, but impressions of lower competence in others <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> .

text.text: Thus, emotional expressivity may calibrate the degree to which happiness-like facial features inform trustworthiness judgments, i.e., the magnitude of emotion overgeneralization.

At the individual level, even when broader social ecology is held constant, individuals differ in their personal histories of encountering expression-intention pairings, shaped by, for example, family expressivity norms, occupational context, and the composition of one's social network.
There is substantial interindividual variation within countries in perceptions of emotional expressivity norms 32 .
text.formatted: There is substantial interindividual variation within countries in perceptions of emotional expressivity norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> .

text.text: Those who perceive their environment as more expressively open have therefore been more consistently exposed to authentic smiling as a signal of benevolent intentions, strengthening their mappings between happiness-related cues and trustworthiness.

Importantly, however, the consequences of individual differences in expressivity perceptions may depend on the broader cultural ecology in which these experiences occur: individual exposure to expressive cues should be most predictive of emotion overgeneralization when such cues are reliable and informative.

The present registered report provides a cross-cultural test of whether emotion overgeneralization in face-based trustworthiness judgments varies as a function of emotional expressivity at both the country and individual levels.
We will collect data from approximately 6,400 participants across 32 countries spanning all inhabited continents (Figure 1).
text.formatted: We will collect data from approximately 6,400 participants across 32 countries spanning all inhabited continents (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Participants will evaluate the trustworthiness of unfamiliar individuals from standardized resting facial photographs and complete a measure of emotional expressivity using the Abridged Display Rule Assessment Inventory 32, 33 .
text.formatted: Participants will evaluate the trustworthiness of unfamiliar individuals from standardized resting facial photographs and complete a measure of emotional expressivity using the Abridged Display Rule Assessment Inventory <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> .

text.text: Computational modeling will quantify each face's resemblance to happiness-related facial configurations using a validated deep learning-based tool 34.
text.formatted: Computational modeling will quantify each face's resemblance to happiness-related facial configurations using a validated deep learning-based tool <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34</ref>.

text.text: As shown in Table 1, at the country level, we test whether cultural differences in emotional expressivity are associated with variation in emotion overgeneralization.
text.formatted: As shown in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>, at the country level, we test whether cultural differences in emotional expressivity are associated with variation in emotion overgeneralization.

text.text: We hypothesize that individuals from countries higher in emotional expressivity will show stronger emotion overgeneralization, such that the association between happiness-resemblance scores and trustworthiness ratings will be stronger (H1).
At the individual level, we test whether individual emotional expressivity is associated with emotion overgeneralization within countries.
We hypothesize that within countries, individuals who have greater emotional expressivity will show stronger emotion overgeneralization (H2).
Finally, as an exploratory analysis, we examine whether cultural context moderates the relationship between individual-level emotional expressivity and emotion overgeneralization.

We predict that the positive association between individual emotional expressivity and emotion overgeneralization will be stronger in countries higher in emotional expressivity. selected for data collection are highlighted, with color indicating country-level emotional expressivity derived from Matsumoto's cross-cultural data 32 , where available.
Countries without available expressivity data are shown in grey.

Archival values from the 2008 dataset are shown to illustrate the expressivity range spanned by our country selection; for actual analysis, we will use DRAI scores collected in the present study, allowing us to examine emotional expressivity at both the individual level and the country level across all 32 countries.
The present research complies with all relevant ethical regulations.
It has been approved by the Institutional Review Board of the National University of Singapore (NUS-IRB-2024-241 and DERC-000092).
Informed consent will be obtained from all human participants.
Participants will be paid in accordance with the standard of the online panel providers (e.g., Toluna).

In our main study, participants from multiple countries will complete the tasks in the following order: (i) a face-rating task assessing perceived trustworthiness of unfamiliar individuals, (ii) questionnaires assessing emotional expressivity, and (iii) demographic information.

The survey will be translated into the local languages following standard crosscultural translation procedures, including forward translation and back-translation to ensure semantic and conceptual equivalence across language versions.

In addition to measures collected directly from participants, we will include derived measures, such as emotional resemblance scores for each face image (computed using automated facial analysis tools) and ethnic fractionalization (obtained from published, validated indices).
As the study involves no experimental manipulation, all participants complete an identical task sequence, with no betweenor within-subjects conditions.
Trustworthiness ratings.
Participants will rate 120 face images on trustworthiness.
The face stimuli are drawn from prior cross-cultural work 35 and include emotionally neutral, frontfacing adult faces from the Chicago Face Database 36 .
text.formatted: The face stimuli are drawn from prior cross-cultural work <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35</ref> and include emotionally neutral, frontfacing adult faces from the Chicago Face Database <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36</ref> .

text.text: The final set contains equal numbers of male and female faces, and one-fourth each of White, Black, Latino, and Asian faces.
The individuals photographed were instructed to face the camera directly with a neutral expression.
Background, lighting, and clothing were held constant across all images.
Participants will rate the trustworthiness of each face using a scale ranging from 1 (not at all) to 9 (very) at their own pace.
Stimuli will appear in a randomized order.
Emotional resemblance.

Emotional resemblance to happiness will be computed for each face stimulus using Py-Feat with ResMaskNet (Residual Masking Network), which applies a deep residual network combined with U-Net architecture to predict emotion probabilities 34, 37.
text.formatted: Emotional resemblance to happiness will be computed for each face stimulus using Py-Feat with ResMaskNet (Residual Masking Network), which applies a deep residual network combined with U-Net architecture to predict emotion probabilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37</ref>.

text.text: Emotion detectors were trained on an aggregate of diverse datasets encompassing Euro-American, African American, and Asian populations, providing greater demographic representativeness than single-site laboratory collections.
The training protocols further enhance ecological validity by incorporating both laboratory-controlled posed expressions and naturalistic facial behaviors sourced from the internet 37 .
text.formatted: The training protocols further enhance ecological validity by incorporating both laboratory-controlled posed expressions and naturalistic facial behaviors sourced from the internet <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37</ref> .

text.text: These happiness probabilities will be combined with participants' trustworthiness ratings to calculate emotion overgeneralization scores (see Analysis Plan).
Emotional expressivity.

Emotional expressivity will be measured using the Abridged Display Rule Assessment Inventory (DRAI), a psychometrically validated instrument designed to assess normative regulation of emotional expression across multiple interpersonal contexts 32, 33.
text.formatted: Emotional expressivity will be measured using the Abridged Display Rule Assessment Inventory (DRAI), a psychometrically validated instrument designed to assess normative regulation of emotional expression across multiple interpersonal contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref>.

text.text: Expressive norms vary systematically across cultures, with display-rule norms capturing culturally shared expectations regarding emotional expression 32 .
text.formatted: Expressive norms vary systematically across cultures, with display-rule norms capturing culturally shared expectations regarding emotional expression <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> .

text.text: The instrument asks respondents about social norms governing emotional expression when they are alone and when interacting with five different social partners in both public and private settings.
Respondents indicate which of six theoretically derived behaviors is most appropriate when experiencing anger, contempt, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, or surprise.

These response options correspond to the six expression-management modes identified by Ekman and Friesen 38, 39 : "show more than you feel it" (amplification), "express it as you feel it" (expression), "show the emotion while smiling at the same time" (qualification), "show less than you feel it" (deamplification), "hide your feelings by smiling" (masking), and "show nothing" (neutralization).
text.formatted: These response options correspond to the six expression-management modes identified by Ekman and Friesen <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39</ref> : "show more than you feel it" (amplification), "express it as you feel it" (expression), "show the emotion while smiling at the same time" (qualification), "show less than you feel it" (deamplification), "hide your feelings by smiling" (masking), and "show nothing" (neutralization).

text.text: In the present study, we will use the "express it as you feel it" index, defined as the total number of situations in which participants endorse authentic emotional expression.
Here, we focus not simply on the overall frequency of emotional displays, but on the frequency of expressions that reliably co-occur with genuine internal states.
Such expressions are more informative for learning expression-intention associations, whereas purely strategic or exaggerated displays introduce noise.
Learning depends not only on the diagnosticity of a signal (i.e., accuracy) but also on the frequency of exposure to reliable pairings.
Even when a signal is highly diagnostic (e.g., a rare smile is likely to be authentic), limited exposure to such pairings may constrain the formation of strong overgeneralized heuristics.

We selected this index rather than the broader overall expressivity measure because it more directly captures normative endorsement of genuine emotional display, rather than tendencies toward amplification or suppression.
Individual total scores will serve as the individual-level indicator, and country-level indicators will be derived by aggregating individual scores within each country.
We will ask participants to report their gender, age, country of birth, length of stay in the country of data collection, and ethnic background.

All demographic materials will be adjusted to the respective sites by local collaborators, ensuring that our questions will assess locally meaningful categories (e.g., ethnic background will be excluded in sites where the local political climate may prevent participants from sharing such information).

To account for potential confounding effects of cross-racial familiarity on participants' trait ratings, which may vary across countries despite a standardized stimulus set, we will include a measure of ethnic fractionalization 40 .
text.formatted: To account for potential confounding effects of cross-racial familiarity on participants' trait ratings, which may vary across countries despite a standardized stimulus set, we will include a measure of ethnic fractionalization <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">40</ref> .

text.text: This measure quantifies each country's ethnic heterogeneity as one minus the Herfindahl index of group shares, reflecting the probability of two randomly selected individuals from a population belonging to different ethnic groups.
Higher fractionalization indicates greater ethnic diversity within a country.

We include ethnic fractionalization as a country-level covariate to absorb cross-country differences in everyday face-exposure ecology, which could influence baseline trait calibration through mechanisms such as familiar face overgeneralization 15 ; we do not have a directional prediction for its association with overgeneralization.
text.formatted: We include ethnic fractionalization as a country-level covariate to absorb cross-country differences in everyday face-exposure ecology, which could influence baseline trait calibration through mechanisms such as familiar face overgeneralization <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> ; we do not have a directional prediction for its association with overgeneralization.

text.text: Sampling strategy.
We plan to recruit participants from 32 countries worldwide (see Figure 1) through Toluna, with other established online panel providers used as backups.
text.formatted: We plan to recruit participants from 32 countries worldwide (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>) through Toluna, with other established online panel providers used as backups.

text.text: Within each country, the sampling will be stratified by gender, age (18-65 years), and region (where feasible).
Countries were selected to capture broad cross-national variation in emotional expressivity while ensuring geographic coverage 41 .
text.formatted: Countries were selected to capture broad cross-national variation in emotional expressivity while ensuring geographic coverage <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> .

text.text: In addition, the selection includes countries that vary substantially on established cultural dimensions (e.g., individualism-collectivism 42, 43 and cultural distance from the United States 44 ) and cultural clusters (based on World Values Survey groupings 45, 46 ).
text.formatted: In addition, the selection includes countries that vary substantially on established cultural dimensions (e.g., individualism-collectivism <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43</ref> and cultural distance from the United States <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44</ref> ) and cultural clusters (based on World Values Survey groupings <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">45,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">46</ref> ).

text.text: This diversity in cultural and psychological dimensions is illustrated in Table S3 and Figure S2.
text.formatted: This diversity in cultural and psychological dimensions is illustrated in Table <ref type="table">S3</ref> and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">S2</ref>.

text.text: Further details on country selection are provided in the Supplementary Information.
We conducted a series of power analyses to determine an appropriate number of both countries (K = 20, 25, 30, 32) and participants per country (N = 150, 200, 250, 300).
To assess the expected power, we set α = .05.
We used the simr package in R to run 1,000 simulations of the planned mixed-models specified in our analysis plan 47 .
text.formatted: We used the simr package in R to run 1,000 simulations of the planned mixed-models specified in our analysis plan <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47</ref> .

text.text: Model parameters were estimated based on previous literature and our pilot study.
The simulations utilized the Kenward-Roger approximation for fixed effects testing to ensure robustness.
See the Supplementary Information for power curves for both hypotheses across the full parameter space.
For H1, we examined the effect of country-level expressivity on face-based overgeneralization.
As this hypothesis involves a level-2 predictor, power is primarily driven by the number of countries (K) rather than the number of participants (N).
With K = 30 and N = 200, the estimated power was 93.6%, slightly below the prespecified 95% threshold.
We therefore increased the number of countries to K = 32, which yielded 95.2% power for this effect (Figure S3).
text.formatted: We therefore increased the number of countries to K = 32, which yielded 95.2% power for this effect (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">S3</ref>).

text.text: K = 32 is also comparable to, or larger than, those commonly used in cross-cultural psychological research 48, 49.
text.formatted: K = 32 is also comparable to, or larger than, those commonly used in cross-cultural psychological research <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">48,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">49</ref>.

text.text: For H2, we considered the effect of individual-level expressivity on overgeneralization.
To isolate the within-country effect, this predictor was group-mean centered within each country.
We conducted a sensitivity analysis by varying the effect size (b = 0.05, 0.10, 0.15) and the random slope variance for expressivity (0.0064, 0.0144, 0.0256).

We specifically tested a slope variance of 0.0144 (SD = 0.12) as a conservative estimate; this value accounts for potential cultural heterogeneity where approximately 20% of countries might theoretically exhibit an association in the opposite direction.
At K = 32 and N = 200, we achieved power > 95% for a small effect of b = 0.10 even under a conservative variance assumption of 0.0144 (Figure S4).
text.formatted: At K = 32 and N = 200, we achieved power > 95% for a small effect of b = 0.10 even under a conservative variance assumption of 0.0144 (Figure <ref type="figure">S4</ref>).

text.text: In sum, these simulations suggest that a sample of 200 participants per country across 32 countries (N = 6,400) provides sufficient power to detect our primary effects of interest.
This target ensures we are well-powered for individual-level effects while maintaining a rigorous and feasible sample for country-level comparisons.
Inclusion and exclusion criteria.
Participants must have normal or corrected-to-normal vision and must have been born in, and currently residing in, the country where data are collected.

To ensure data quality, exclusion will be applied if a participant meets any of the following criteria: (a) provides identical ratings on more than 90% of face-rating trials; (b) uses only two response options across all trait-rating trials, indicating a binary response pattern; or (c) fails all embedded attention checks.
We target 200 analyzable participants per country (N = 6,400) and will oversample by 10% to account for expected participant exclusions.
All analyses will be performed in R 50 .
text.formatted: All analyses will be performed in R <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">50</ref> .

text.text: We operationalize emotion overgeneralization as a within-person association between stimulus-level happiness resemblance and trustworthiness ratings, which is invariant to individual differences in overall rating level.

Specifically, for each participant, emotion overgeneralization will be indexed as the Pearson correlation coefficient between their trustworthiness ratings and the happiness resemblance scores of the 120 face stimuli.
These individual-level correlation coefficients will be Fisher z-transformed prior to all inferential analyses and will serve as the primary dependent variable in all models.
This index is the participant-specific slope relating happiness resemblance to trustworthiness ratings.

Modeling this slope as a function of expressivity therefore tests whether the association between happiness resemblance and trustworthiness ratings varies as a function of expressivity, providing an intuitive participant-level summary while remaining closely aligned with the corresponding cross-level interaction in a trial-level model.
Outcome-neutral data quality checks.
Before testing the preregistered hypotheses, we will conduct two outcome-neutral checks to assess whether the data provide a suitable basis for the planned analyses.
First, we will test whether, when pooling across countries, happiness resemblance is positively associated with perceived trustworthiness.
This analysis serves as a positive control to establish that the expected association between facial resemblance to happiness and trustworthiness is detectable in the overall sample.
Second, we will report between-country variance in emotional expressivity scores to characterize the extent of crosscountry variation.
These checks are independent of the hypothesized associations between emotional expressivity and emotion overgeneralization.

To test country-level hypothesis H1, whether country-level emotional expressivity is associated with cross-national variation in emotion overgeneralization, we will fit a multilevel linear model with individuals (Level 1) nested within countries (Level 2).
The dependent variable will be individual Fisher z-transformed emotion overgeneralization scores.
The key predictor will be country-level mean emotional expressivity (Level 2).
Countries will be included as random intercepts.
Random slopes will not be specified because the predictor is defined at the country level and does not vary within countries.
Participant age and gender (Level 1), and ethnic fractionalization (Level 2) will be included as covariates.
Individual-level analyses.
We will test individual-level hypothesis H2, whether individuals who perceive greater normative emotional expressivity will show stronger emotion overgeneralization.
The dependent variable will be Fisher z-transformed emotion overgeneralization.

The model will include group-mean centered individual expressivity (main predictor; within-country effect) and the corresponding country mean (to account for the between-country effect) to separate within-and between-country associations.
Covariates will include participant age and gender (Level 1), and ethnic fractionalization (Level 2).
Countries will be included as random effects.

If the maximal random-effects structure fails to converge or produces singular fits, we will simplify the model following standard guidance for handling convergence failure in mixed models 51, 52 , retaining a model with random intercepts for countries if further simplification is required.
text.formatted: If the maximal random-effects structure fails to converge or produces singular fits, we will simplify the model following standard guidance for handling convergence failure in mixed models <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">51,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">52</ref> , retaining a model with random intercepts for countries if further simplification is required.

text.text: As an exploratory analysis, we will examine whether country-level emotional expressivity moderates the association between individual emotional expressivity and emotion overgeneralization by fitting a multilevel linear model that includes the interaction between individual-level emotional expressivity and countrylevel mean emotional expressivity.
Individual expressivity will be group-mean centered to capture within-country individual differences, whereas country-level emotional expressivity will be grand-mean centered.
The dependent variable will be Fisher z-transformed emotion overgeneralization.
Participant age and gender (Level 1), and ethnic fractionalization (Level 2) will be included as covariates.
Countries will be included as random effects.
Robustness checks.
We will compute overgeneralization separately within each face-race subset (White/Black/Latino/Asian; 30 faces each).
Because each subset contains only 30 faces, participant-level estimates of overgeneralization may be less stable.

We will therefore aggregate trustworthiness ratings at the country level before computing overgeneralization separately for each subset, and examine whether the country-level association replicates in direction across subsets.
We will also use norming data from the Chicago Face Database as an alternative proxy for perceived happiness resemblance and re-run the analyses to evaluate the robustness of the findings.

To demonstrate the feasibility of our study design and analytic strategy for H1, we integrated two existing cross-cultural datasets: emotional expressivity scores from a prior study using the Display Rule Assessment Inventory 32 , and large-scale, face-based trustworthiness judgments from the Psychological Science Accelerator (PSA) project 35 .

text.text: In the pilot data, emotional expressivity was operationalized as the total number of situations in which participants selected "express it as you feel it" as the most appropriate behavior across social scenarios, excluding the "amplify" responses that are included in the overall expressivity index.
Twenty-one countries overlapped across datasets.
Among the more than 10,000 participants in the PSA face perception dataset, each participant rated a single trait that was randomly assigned.
Of these, 531 rated trustworthiness.
For each face stimulus, structural resemblance to happiness was estimated using Py-Feat.
Emotion overgeneralization was operationalized as the Fisher z-transformed correlation between happiness resemblance scores and trustworthiness ratings.

Because the expressivity predictor in this existing dataset is only available as a national aggregate, we first examined overgeneralization at the country level by aggregating trustworthiness ratings within each country.

Greater endorsement of expressing emotions "as felt" predicted stronger emotion overgeneralization, b = 0.47, 95% CI [0.03, 0.90], SE = 0.21, t(18) = 2.27, p = .036, controlling for ethnic fractionalization, which serves as a proxy for cross-racial familiarity that may influence participants' trait ratings (Figure 2).

text.text: However, the number of participants contributing trustworthiness ratings varied substantially across countries (Figure S1).
text.formatted: However, the number of participants contributing trustworthiness ratings varied substantially across countries (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">S1</ref>).

text.text: To account for this imbalance and retain the full participant-level information, we additionally analyzed the raw ratings using a mixed-effects model with participants nested within countries.
Controlling for regional ethnic fractionalization, age, and gender, the association remained positive, b = 0.16, 95% CI [0.01, 0.32], SE = 0.07, t(10.4) = 2.29, p = .044.
Full analytic details are reported in the Supplementary Information.
Importantly, this effect emerged only for the "express it as you feel it" index.

Emotion overgeneralization was not significantly associated with the broader overall expressivity measure, which combines responses across multiple display strategies (e.g., dissimulating, expressing as felt, and amplifying).
This pattern suggests that the relationship might reflect the diagnostic value attributed to authentic emotional expressions rather than the general prevalence or amplification of emotional displays.
Full analyses using the overall expressivity index are reported in the Supplementary Information.

To address concerns that cross-cultural differences in emotion perception might compromise the comparability of automated emotion-resemblance estimates, we compared models allowing sites (i.e., countries; Hong Kong included as a separate site where available) to vary in overall rating intensity (random intercepts) versus models allowing variation in sensitivity to structural cues (random slopes; see Supplementary Information).

Model comparison indicated no evidence for cross-site slope variation, supporting the cross-site comparability of Py-Featderived resemblance scores for use as inputs when estimating emotion overgeneralization within each country.
These pilot results illustrate that the proposed operationalization and analytic framework can detect cultural variation in emotion overgeneralization.

However, participant sample sizes varied widely across countries in the PSA face perception dataset, with some countries contributing fewer than 10 participants (see Figure S1), making these estimates necessarily preliminary and potentially subject to instability.
text.formatted: However, participant sample sizes varied widely across countries in the PSA face perception dataset, with some countries contributing fewer than 10 participants (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">S1</ref>), making these estimates necessarily preliminary and potentially subject to instability.

text.text: Meanwhile, the composition of pilot samples likely varied across sites (e.g., student vs. general-population recruitment), introducing heterogeneity beyond sample size that further limits cross-country comparability.

The planned study addresses this limitation directly by targeting equal samples of N = 200 per country and recruiting through quota-balanced panels with comparable demographic composition across sites (see Sampling strategy).

Moreover, although there was substantial interindividual variation in emotional expressivity norm perception within countries 32 , the available data did not allow us to examine individual-level associations, as the emotional expressivity and face perception datasets were collected at different time points and were not obtained from the same individuals.

This section provides detailed analytic procedures for the pilot analyses described in the main text.

To evaluate the feasibility of the proposed operationalization and analytic framework for testing the main hypothesis H1, we conducted pilot analyses linking cross-cultural emotional expressivity norms to large-scale face-based trustworthiness judgments.

Emotional expressivity scores were drawn from a prior cross-cultural study assessing display rule norms across 32 countries and regions (including Hong Kong, a Special Administrative Region of China) using the Display Rule Assessment Inventory (DRAI) 32 .

text.text: The DRAI measures normative regulation of emotional expression across multiple interaction contexts.
The present pilot used the "express it as you feel it" index, defined as the total number of situations in which participants endorsed authentic emotional expression.

We selected this index over the broader overall expressivity measure because it more directly captures normative endorsement of genuine emotional display rather than amplification or suppression tendencies.
Of the 32 sites in the original dataset, 21 overlapped with the face-rating dataset described below.

Trustworthiness ratings were obtained from the Psychological Science Accelerator (PSA) project 35 , which collected trait judgments across 43 countries and regions using 120 standardized face images from the Chicago Face Database 36 .

For each of the 120 face stimuli, structural resemblance to happiness was estimated using Py-Feat, yielding a probability score reflecting resemblance to happiness-related facial configurations.
Emotion overgeneralization was operationalized as the association between happiness resemblance scores and trustworthiness judgments across faces.
Because the expressivity predictor was only available as a national aggregate, we computed overgeneralization using two complementary estimators.

First, using raw participant trustworthiness ratings, emotion overgeneralization was calculated separately for each participant by correlating their ratings with the corresponding happiness resemblance scores across faces, with correlations Fisher z-transformed prior to analysis.
Second, using an aggregated approach, trustworthiness ratings were first averaged across participants within each country for each face stimulus to reduce participant-level noise.
Pearson correlations were then computed between happiness resemblance scores and these aggregated trustworthiness ratings across the 120 faces.
The resulting correlation coefficients were also Fisher z-transformed.
Linear regression of aggregated ratings.

Because the emotional expressivity predictor is available only at the national level in this dataset, we first examined the relationship between emotional expressivity and emotion overgeneralization using country-level aggregated ratings (N = 21 countries).
Emotion overgeneralization scores were computed by aggregating participant trustworthiness ratings within each country.
We estimated ordinary least squares regression models predicting aggregated emotion overgeneralization from national emotional expressivity.
For each expressivity measure, we estimated both a simple model, including emotional expressivity as the sole predictor, and a full model, additionally controlling for ethnic fractionalization.
Results from both models are reported in Table S1.

text.text: For the "express it as you feel it" index, higher endorsement of expressing emotions as felt was associated with stronger emotion overgeneralization (full model: b = 0.47, 95% CI [0.03, 0.90], SE = 0.21, t(18) = 2.27, p = .036).

In contrast, the overall expressivity measure-capturing the extent to which individuals believe they should conceal, freely express, or amplify emotional expressions-was not significantly associated with emotion overgeneralization in either the simple or full models (Table S1).

Together, both estimators converge on the same directional pattern, suggesting that the proposed analytic framework can detect cross-national variation in emotion overgeneralization despite differences in sample size and aggregation level.
With substantially larger and more balanced samples per country in the planned study (N = 200 per country), these estimates should be considerably more precise.

A potential methodological concern is that cultures may differ not only in how much they overgeneralize emotion to trait judgments, but in how they perceive the emotional content of faces in the first place.

If the mapping between structural resemblance and perceived emotion varies across countries and regions, then Py-Feat-derived scores would not function as a comparable input across countries, confounding any cross-cultural comparison of overgeneralization.

To ensure that Py-Feat-derived structural resemblance scores are comparably linked to emotion perceptions across countries and regions, we tested whether cross-cultural differences in emotion judgments reflected overall rating intensity (intercepts) or differential sensitivity to structural resemblance (slopes).
We compared a random-intercept model with a model including Model comparison indicated no evidence for random slope variation, Δχ²(2) = 0.29, p = .867.

These results suggest that cross-cultural differences are primarily reflected in overall rating intensity rather than heterogeneous slopes linking structural emotion resemblance to perceived emotions.

Because our primary interest lies in correlations between Py-Feat-derived resemblance scores and trustworthiness judgments, variation in intercepts does not affect our inferences, whereas variation in slopes would.
Accordingly, this analysis supports the cross-site comparability of Py-Feat-derived resemblance scores (i.e., measurement consistency) as inputs in our main analyses.

Note that this check pertains specifically to the mapping between Py-Featderived resemblance scores and explicit emotion perceptions, and therefore does not address whether emotion overgeneralization (i.e., structural resemblance → trustworthiness) varies across countries, which is the focus of our preregistered hypotheses.

text.text: Full simulation code and output tables are provided to facilitate reproducibility (see the Code Availability section).
All simulations used 1,000 iterations, with statistical significance evaluated at α = .05 and fixed effects tested using the Kenward-Roger approximation.

Power was estimated across a range of design parameters, including the number of countries (K = 20, 25, 30, 32), the number of participants per country (N = 150, 200, 250, 300), and plausible effect sizes informed by pilot data and prior literature.
For H1, the primary simulation used an expected effect of b = 0.16, based on the pilot study.
For H2, we additionally varied the random slope variance for individual-level expressivity (0.0064, 0.0144, 0.0256), corresponding to slope standard deviations of 0.08, 0.12, and 0.16.

Assuming a main effect of b = 0.10, these variance levels correspond to three theoretical distributions: specifically, a variance of 0.0064 (SD = 0.08) models a scenario of baseline heterogeneity, where the effect is positive in approximately 90% of sampled countries.
A variance of 0.0144 (SD = 0.12) represents moderate cultural moderation, where the effect is positive in 80% of cultures but reverses in 20%.

Finally, a variance of 0.0256 (SD = 0.16) reflects higher cultural moderation, where specific contextual factors (e.g., distinct cultural norms) drive effect reversals in approximately 30% of the countries.
Power curves across the full parameter space are presented in Figure S3 (H1) and Figure S4 (H2).
